videos.title: Castr poster-style launch trailer
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (one lowercase word), a 4-word tagline, the 3-step story of what it does, a launch date and domain, a royalty-free song with a clear drop, 4 vertical talking-to-camera clips and 12 portrait photos. If I skip any, use the defaults: "castr", "ugc ads, cast by ai", write a brief → scan 1,000 creators → cast 4, Mixkit "Cat Walk" (129.6 BPM, drop at 29.7s), free Pexels clips and portraits, and transparent stickers from Pixabay (serum, mic, megaphone, vintage camera, spotlight, lips).
</inputs>

<direction>
A 25 second square launch trailer, 1440x1440 at 60fps, loud poster style. Cobalt #2B3BFF, ink #0E0F1F, cream #F6E4C6, pink #FF7DC7, tangerine #FF5A1F. Archivo 900 extra-condensed for names, expanded for headlines, Geist and Geist Mono for labels. Op-art sunburst, scrolling waves, film grain. Real media only: the clips play inside the design, and the stickers get a white die-cut border and a soft shadow.
Motion rules: the camera never stops (a slow 1.03-1.07 push on every scene), nothing pops in (letters rise through a mask line one by one), nothing snaps to the beat (patterns rotate continuously), swaps are carousel glides of about 0.55s, colour changes fade over about 0.35s, stickers ease in and then keep a slow sway. No full stops after the wordmark or any headline.
Banned: beat-snapped rotations, pop-in slams, white flashes, crossfades between scenes, hard cuts, templates.
</direction>

<structure>
54 beats. The song starts 8 beats before its drop.
Beats 0-8: a cobalt sunburst turns around a breathing cream disc. The wordmark types in with a gliding caret and the tagline pill rises. The disc floods the frame into the drop.
Beat 8, the drop: the cream becomes the face of a 3D box and "ONE BRIEF" rises letter by letter. The camera pulls back to the box floating on waves. On beat 12 it turns to "1,000 CREATORS" (stacked, with outlined echoes), on beat 14 to "ZERO DMs".
Beats 16-22: a whip to a dark desk. A tangerine "BRIEF #042" ticket types its rows (product, vibe, cast, due), stickers drift on, a polaroid of a real clip drops onto the corner, and a "NOW CASTING" stamp presses down on beat 20.
Beats 22-34: the casting stage. A crowd of black and white portraits in an arc, a 3D stage block, and the creators gliding through like a carousel. Each plays live in a big disc in black and white, with their name in pink on the stage, their followers, and a MATCH % that counts up. One beat later a "CAST ✓" stamp lands and the clip fades to colour. A counter rolls 1/4 to 4/4.
Beats 34-39: pink floods out of the last disc. The disc morphs into a phone screen (the clip keeps playing) and fans into 4 phones playing all 4 creators, with views counting up. "4 ADS" and "BY FRIDAY" rise.
Beats 39-44, the music's break: the pink floor drops away and a cream "JOIN THE WAITLIST" ticket glides down onto the sunburst. On the pickup its stub tears off.
Beats 44-54: the ticket body morphs into a poster arch. The wordmark rises in, then the tagline, then an info bar slides up in 3 blocks (date, numbers, domain) and a ticker runs round the frame edge. Then it all folds back into the opening disc, so the last frame is the first.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Every frame is a pure function of time inside seek(t).
2. A beat map in beats, B = 60/BPM, with the song placed so its drop lands on beat 8.
3. The 3D box is an orthographic projection: each face is a 1440px offscreen canvas drawn with an affine transform and shaded by its normal.
4. Cut the clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg, draw frame floor(t*30), and do the black and white with ctx.filter.
5. Trim the sticker PNGs and add the die-cut border by dilating their alpha.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event (a shutter on every cast, whooshes on the glides, key clicks on the typing), each placed by its measured peak. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 8 motion-blur subframes. Scan for single-frame pops, then compare its motion against a reference video (hard jumps per second, share of still frames).
</build>

<gotchas>
A pattern that rotates one notch per beat reads as stutter: rotate it continuously, and pick each ring's speed so it lands on the same pattern at the last frame. 4 subframes ghost on fast whips, so use 8. A layer whose background is a huge flood circle still covers the screen after sliding down one frame height, so switch it to a full-frame rect once it has flooded. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's. The disc must morph inside the same camera transform as the scene it leaves, or it jumps.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, box, brief, casting, phones, poster) before you render.
</start>

videos.title: Papery illustrated music video
videos.prompt:
Make a complete music video for the song in this folder, with all
visuals drawn and animated in JavaScript. Use the entire song.

SETUP
Inspect this folder and identify the song and any lyrics or reference
files. Preserve my original files unchanged.

Use this existing animation starter:
https://t.co/oN3A7ZZyEl

Clone it into a new ./video subfolder, unless an existing copy is
already present. Do not overwrite existing work or clone into the
nonempty project root.

Read its README.md and ANIMATION_GUIDE.md completely, then inspect
render.mjs and the project configuration. Use the existing rendering
machinery rather than inventing a replacement.

Check Node.js, Chrome, and FFmpeg. Inspect the package configuration
and install the project dependencies. Ask before making system-wide
changes or downloading large additional tools.

Do not use fal, external image/video generation, paid APIs, or the
hybrid music-video plugin. All finished visuals must be code-drawn.

CREATIVE DIRECTION
Create a cohesive, visually imaginative animated music video with a
handmade, papery, illustrated feel. Express the song's meaning through
scenes, characters, visual metaphors, and purposeful transitions.
Establish an engaging opening and develop recurring visual motifs.
Do not make a slideshow, a generic audio visualizer, or one animation
loop repeated for the entire song. Design characters appropriate to
this song rather than automatically using the starter's mascot.

MUSIC AND TIMING
Use the supplied recording as the continuous master soundtrack.
Do not remix, replace, speed up, or shorten it.

Measure its duration and use available local audio-analysis tools to
identify musical sections and likely beat/accent timings. Record these
in a shared timeline and drive animation from that timeline.

Use supplied lyrics as authoritative. If lyrics are missing, use a
local transcription tool only if available, flag uncertain words, and
do not invent lyrics. Continue with non-lyric visuals where necessary.

When verified lyrics are available, use expressive, readable lyric
animation where it strengthens the scene. This explicitly overrides
the starter's default preference against lettering.

PRODUCTION
Write STORYBOARD.md with timed scenes covering the complete recording.
Save the project brief and rerender instructions in CLAUDE.md.

Then build the video. Make reasonable creative decisions and continue
without stopping for approval at every scene.

Test a few representative frames and a short section before the full
render. Inspect the resulting images and frame sequences, fix visible
defects, and keep the animation practical for this computer.

Use efficient code-drawn textures if expensive watercolor effects
make rendering impractical.

DELIVERY
Render the complete video

videos.title: LOUD ONE launch film
videos.prompt:
<inputs>

Defaults: product name LOUD ONE; 1920 × 1080; 30 fps; exactly 24 seconds and 720 frames; a cobalt-blue handheld music device with a large orange control, black LED display, speaker grille, silver hardware, and connected red and black cables.

Keep the reference's on-device copy unless replacement copy is supplied. Treat the preorder message as artwork for this recreation; do not invent a working purchase link.
</inputs>

<direction>
Create an energetic, glossy 3D product film with Higgsfield Katana and Claude Motion. The central idea is that a hummed idea travels through a playful world of musical hardware and becomes something ready to share.

The journey is HUM → SHAPE → DROP, ending with LOUD ONE.

Build a coherent floating installation in an open blue environment. The camera travels between physical objects suspended around a tall chrome mast: the hero device, speech-bubble display, horns, a recording light, meter, cassette, speaker stack, and LED letter panels.

The background is a saturated sky-blue to pale blue-gray gradient. Keep it spacious and luminous. There is no room, floor, horizon line, editor panel, or storyboard strip.

Use rounded industrial design, polished colored plastic, brushed and polished metal, dark rubber, and black perforated display surfaces. Objects should feel fabricated and dimensional even when their arrangement is playful.

Approximate palette: cobalt #173BD5, sky blue #158CEC, pale blue-gray #DCEAF1, orange #F34A13, cream #E8E5DE, violet #7137C4, lime #A9D53C, amber #E5AD35, and near-black #10151C. Refine against the reference.

Light the scene with large soft sources and sharp enough reflections to reveal the materials. Keep contact shadows between assembled parts. Preserve bright chrome highlights without losing detail in the white housing.

Use wide-angle product cinematography: close passes, changing perspective, orbiting, foreground occlusion, tilts, and fast travel between stations. Slow down when a message needs to be read.

Most typography belongs on physical objects. LED lettering should be made from a consistent dot grid. The main device types in white with an orange cursor; speech-bubble screens use warm-white dots, with orange emphasis; directional signs use amber.

Maintain the small HIGGSFIELD / CLAUDE MOTION badge at the upper-right as a separate overlay. Keep it fixed while the camera moves.

Avoid flat screenshots pretending to be 3D, unrelated montage inserts, excessive lens distortion, random glitch effects, or floating text detached from the objects.
</direction>

<structure>
Use these approximate reconstruction beats. Refine transitions against the reference while preserving the full 24-second runtime.

0:00–0:02.6 / HUM INTO THE DEVICE
Open close to the cobalt-blue hero device at an angle. Its rounded rectangular housing fills much of the image.

Show the recessed black LED display, speaker slots, small circular metal grille, top cable connections, LOUD ONE label, and large orange circular control surrounded by a ridged silver ring.

Type “hum me something...” across the display with an orange insertion cursor. Reveal the lettering as discrete LED states. As the camera approaches, change the screen to a recording treatment with a red REC indicator and an orange waveform.

Move across the front toward the orange control. Let changing reflections reveal the blue casing and machined ring. Keep the device stable as a rigid object.

0:02.6–0:05.6 / EVERY HIT STARTS AS A HUM
Pull away and travel toward a cream speech-bubble-shaped display mounted high on the chrome mast.

The housing has a soft rectangular screen and a pointed lower-left tail. A thin antenna extends upward; a black cable and red coiled cable connect below.

Begin with an empty black display, then reveal:
“EVERY HIT
STARTS AS A HUM.”

Use warm-white pixel lettering, centered inside the physical screen. Arrive at a readable angle and hold the finished sentence briefly.

Below the display, show a dark metal collar and several small colorful horn speakers. Keep the mechanical connections plausible.

0:05.6–0:08.2 / FOLLOW THE SOUND
Move down and around the mast. Pass the horn cluster, chrome brackets, exposed connectors, and coiled wires.

Reveal a glowing red “ON AIR” sign. Continue past a vertical meter containing circular lamps that rise through green, yellow, and red.

Use changes in distance and perspective to connect the objects. Let the hero device remain visible farther away on its cables.

Add a few suspended green and purple waveform-like squiggles, but keep them secondary. Use the mast, cables, and nearby objects to preserve spatial orientation through the fast camera travel.

0:08.2–0:10.6 / SHAPE IT
Travel toward a large floating cassette. Show it turning from an oblique view into a readable frontal presentation.

Build a dark blue-gray shell with a cream label, two visible reels, transparent windows, screws, seams, and an orange slider along the upper edge.

Main label:
“SHAPE IT.”

Small selectable style labels:
“LO-FI”
“HOUSE”
“FUNK”
“DISCO”

Move the orange control across the choices while the cassette shifts slightly in space. Give the reels subtle rotation. Preserve crisp readable text and realistic thickness at the casing edges.

Use a passing edge or fast turn to carry the camera into the next station.

0:10.6–0:13.5 / DROP IT
Find a narrow black LED sign above a floating audio stack.

Animate amber directional arrows into:
“DROP IT.”

Travel down the stack. Include a small black speaker, a purple rectangular unit, a yellow drum-like speaker body, a cream speaker with an orange cone, and a broad cobalt unit at the bottom.

Add a glossy red exclamation mark beneath the stack. Let the objects respond with controlled movement as the camera passes.

Keep speaker cones circular and their movement axial. Make this section feel like the energy of the musical idea has increased.

0:13.5–0:16.4 / SPELL OUT LOUD
Swing across a group of separate square black LED panels mounted along slender supports.

Reveal the letters L, O, U, D in amber dots. Individual panels rotate or pass through different orientations as the camera moves.

The letters should be legible at their key moments, with the full arrangement becoming understandable through the travel. Maintain the same world, lighting, and hardware language.

Use a fast but readable camera arc to return toward the speech-bubble display. Let a few rounded orange and purple shapes pass in the foreground.

0:16.4–0:20.4 / IDEAS, OUT LOUD
Return to the cream speech-bubble display.

Briefly show a small waveform, then reveal:
“IDEAS,
OUT LOUD.”

Keep IDEAS and OUT warm white. Make LOUD orange.

Hold a readable three-quarter view while the installation moves subtly. Keep the horn cluster, collar, hanging cables, green squiggle, and distant DROP IT sign visible as secondary details.

Near the end of this section, change the display to:
“LOUD
ONE”

Use a fast pullback to reconnect the display with the wider installation.

0:20.4–0:24 / PRODUCT HERO
Bring the cobalt device back into the foreground, suspended by its black and red cables.

Settle it left of center at a flattering three-quarter angle. The large orange control, chrome ring, speaker slots, and rounded casing must remain recognizable.

Place the four amber LED letter panels spelling LOUD to the right, arranged along their slender supports.

Change the device display from “LOUD ONE” to “PRE-ORDER NOW.”

End with a readable hero composition and subtle residual movement. Hold long enough to recognize the product and CTA. Do not force a loop or add an unrelated end card.
</structure>

<build>
1. Use an editable 3D scene and camera in the supported Katana/Claude Motion workflow. Three-dimensional objects must retain their shapes during camera travel. Use the available 3D renderer or supported scene pipeline rather than flattening the whole film into image cards.

2. Build a reusable asset library: hero device, orange dial, LED display surface, speech-bubble housing, mast, horns, ON AIR sign, meter, cassette and slider, speaker components, letter panels, cables, and decorative waveform shapes.

3. Keep geometry, materials, displayed text, lights, camera paths, animation, and branding individually editable. Centralize product name, messages, colors, and beat timings.

4. Place all stations in a shared scene. Plan the camera route before polishing detail. Use foreground objects and whip movements to bridge sections, keeping changes of direction physically understandable.

5. Use a master time function with 720 output frames at 30 fps. Seed randomness. Make each frame directly seekable and repeatable; avoid animation that depends on previous playback.

6. Construct cables with spline-based geometry. Keep endpoints attached to their ports. Give cable curves and suspended devices a small amount of secondary movement that settles after major camera or object actions.

7. Render LED text with proper display-space perspective and a stable dot grid. Use crisp message changes rather than morphing letters into unreadable intermediate glyphs.

8. Use motion blur for fast travel and passing objects, then restore clarity during text holds. Adjust focus for each subject rather than keeping the entire installation equally sharp.

9. Keep the top-right HIGGSFIELD / CLAUDE MOTION badge in screen space. It must not inherit scene blur, perspective, or exposure changes. Supply an unbranded export too if requested.

10. Inspect the supplied audio to place accents. If a new score is needed, propose a playful electronic groove that builds from a simple hummed motif into a fuller arrangement. This is a sound direction, not a claim about the source track.

11. Add focused sound details: a recording click, dial tick, relay or lamp activation, cassette movement, speaker pulse, and restrained pass-by sounds. Let the DROP IT moment receive a stronger musical accent. Keep the final product hold musically resolved.

12. Render a preview first. Check the whole camera route and every text hold before final-quality lighting and export.

Deliver KATANA_Pack_1_LOUD_ONE_1080p_30fps.mp4, the editable project or source, organized assets, and separate audio stems where available.
</build>

<gotchas>
The hero product is LOUD ONE. Do not substitute PHYLLA or the OBSCURA branding from other references.

Keep the large orange dial on the same side of the device throughout. Maintain cable ports, screen placement, grille layout, and physical scale.

LED text lives inside the screens and signs. It must not slide independently of their surfaces.

Do not detach cable ends during the camera moves. Avoid cable intersections with the hero device and screen housing.

The speech-bubble display needs readable front-facing moments. A beautiful extreme angle is not useful if the sentence cannot be read.

Fast camera movement should connect destinations. Avoid random spins with no clear arrival.

Keep the cassette and speaker stack distinct. Preserve the visible style-selection labels and the orange slider.

Chrome reflections must support form. Avoid blown-out rings and shimmering highlights.

The final product hold is part of the film. Do not spend all 24 seconds moving and leave the CTA for a single frame.

No code sidebar, external editor frame, botanical imagery, or extra promotional statistics belong in this reference.
</gotchas>

<start>
Inspect the reference and collect any missing original assets in one question.

Show the asset list, camera route, timing map, and six stills: opening device, speech-bubble message, mast/ON AIR detail, cassette, speaker stack, and final hero.

Build the editable blocking pass, review movement and readability, then finish materials, lighting, sound, and the final render.
</start>

videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: my product's name (nightshift) (one lowercase word, it becomes a black wordmark with a period), the one job a user hands it before bed (book 10 sales calls this week), the three results it reports by morning (200 leads found / 200 emails sent / 10 calls booked), two photos of the same place at night and by day (aligned, so a crossfade reads as a real sunrise), one sunny daytime photo for outside the logo, and a song with a big hit near its start. If I skip any, use the defaults.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 24 second square product launch video, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take that loops. The whole video happens inside the period of the wordmark. Outside it's daytime (the sunny photo behind a black wordmark). Inside it's the night photo under iOS-style glass panels (the blurred photo behind each panel, a tint, a rim light). Nothing cuts: every scene grows out of the last, shapes morph, dots fly, colours change under floods. Every morph glides 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve. Geist, the real macOS pointer, soft shadows that grow with each shape's height.
Banned: flat or gradient backgrounds made in code, camera zooms into tiny points, hard cuts, crossfades between scenes, bouncy springs, particles, glows, holds longer than 1s, cropped type.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's. The song enters on its big hit as the first pill appears.
Open: the letters slide into the period and vanish into it while it glides to the middle. The period opens like an iris onto the night inside it, and "you log off at 6", then "[product] doesn't", roll through one mask line over the night photo.
Ask: a glass "Ask [product]" pill springs in. The cursor clicks it, it glides into an input and the job types out.
Find: send shrinks the input to a dot that ripples into a 23x15 grid. A scan line sweeps it, 200 dots light up and a counter counts them.
Write: the lit dots pour into a glass email composer. A second, purple cursor labelled "[product]" types a personal opener and presses Send, and the counter runs to 200/200.
Night: the composer becomes a glass orb with a progress ring. A clock chip swaps 11:42 PM, 3:17 AM, 5:02 AM, 6:59 AM while the sky relights from night to dawn and "while you sleep" rolls in.
Results (beat 20): the orb turns black and goo-splits into the three result pills. The checks pop green.
Morning: the pills merge into a Dynamic Island that grows into a phone lock screen: the day photo, the date, a big 7:00, the bezel growing out of the screen edge. Three glass notifications stack in, and the cursor taps the first, which opens like iOS.
Proof: a week calendar (10 meetings pop in, a hover shows one's time), then a pipeline chart ($48,200 counts up, the line draws, a hover follows it). A black flood from the line's end becomes "Start your night shift →" and the cursor clicks it.
Out: the button shrinks into a dot, the whole scene closes down into it like an iris, and the letters slide back out of the period. The tagline rises. Last frame = first frame.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML canvas. Everything is a pure function of time inside seek(t): no timers, no state between frames.
2. One element morphs through every state (size, radius, colour, material) from a table of beat times, so retiming is one edit.
3. Render the inside world into an offscreen canvas and reveal it through the period with a circular mask. Never zoom the camera into the dot.
4. Glass: a pre-blurred copy of the photo clipped to the shape, then a tint and a gradient rim.
5. Goo: blur + alpha threshold on an offscreen layer for the split and the merge.
6. Sound: a downloaded SFX for every event, each placed by its measured peak. The song enters on its hit. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
7. Render with Playwright at 60fps with 4 motion-blur subframes. Scan every frame for single-frame jumps and fix each one.
</build>

<gotchas>
A camera zoom into an off-centre dot swings sideways and spikes, so open the dot instead. Ease a closing iris by area, not radius, or its first frames jump. A helper that sets globalAlpha must restore the caller's, or fading cards pop. Counters read the frame's time, not the subframe's, or the digits smear.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and 6 stills (open, find, write, results, phone, out) before you render.
</start>

videos.title: Spotify product film
videos.prompt:
Create a complete, polished Spotify-themed motion graphics video from the following brief. This prompt is self-contained: no reference video or supplied assets are required.

<deliverables> An 18-second MP4 at 1920×1080 and true 60 fps, with music and subtle sound effects Complete editable source Build, render, inspect, and refine the animation before delivering it Do not stop at a storyboard, still images, or an implementation plan </deliverables>
<art_direction>
A premium music-product film presented inside a large, nearly black rounded rectangular stage
The stage occupies roughly 80% of the canvas width and 75% of its height, centered horizontally and slightly below the vertical center
Outside the stage, use a soft atmospheric green background: luminous emerald near the upper-left corner, deeper forest green toward the sides, fading to near-black at the bottom
Inside the stage:
Near-black background
White primary typography
Muted gray secondary text
Spotify green # 1ED760 for emphasis and controls
One clean sans-serif font, such as Geist or Inter
Consistent icon strokes and restrained shadows
Keep compositions compact and centered, with substantial negative space
Text should feel like music-product advertising, not oversized presentation headings
Do not add an outer caption, creator watermark, decorative footer, or progress counter
</art_direction>

<artwork> Create original square album artwork for a fictional track called “Glass Tides” by “AURA”
The hero cover is an abstract macro image of flowing pearlescent liquid silk and molten glass
Use pastel lavender, powder cyan, blush pink, champagne gold, and subtle mint
Include broad three-dimensional folds, realistic reflective highlights, delicate striations, and a prominent sweeping S-shaped fold
Fill the square edge to edge
No text, logo, or border on this hero artwork
Use this same artwork consistently throughout the film

Create additional designed playlist sleeves:
“Late Nights” in mustard yellow
“Good Energy” in pink
“Deep Focus” in blue
“Daily Mix 1”, “Daily Mix 2”, and “Daily Mix 3” in complementary colors

These should look like finished graphic-design covers, with bold typography and simple geometric motifs
</artwork>

<timeline> 0.0–0.6 seconds: A green Spotify icon grows smoothly into the center of the dark stage Give it a confident arrival with minimal overshoot
0.6–1.5 seconds:
The icon transitions into a small Spotify identity above two centered lines:
“Discover”
“new music”
The first line is white; the second is green
Reveal them with short masked vertical movements
1.5–2.4 seconds:
A stylized Spotify desktop interface rises into view
Show a slim sidebar, “Made for you”, three album cards, and small supporting rows
Use a subtle perspective tilt during the entrance, settling toward a frontal view
2.4–3.2 seconds:
Move closer to the three featured covers
Show “New for you” above them
Keep the artwork crisp, with short album titles beneath
A narrow rounded player bar now anchors the bottom of the stage
3.2–4.0 seconds:
The featured cards withdraw into a compact “Fresh finds” list
Reveal four song rows with a slight stagger
Each row contains a thumbnail, short track title, artist, and a small menu icon
4.0–4.9 seconds:
Transition into a horizontal strip of colorful playlist covers
Heading: “Every mood”
Supporting line: “Find what moves you”
The strip slides smoothly sideways, with edge cards partially cropped by the stage
4.9–5.8 seconds:
A compact search field appears
Type “Glass Tides”
Reveal one selected result beneath it, with the iridescent artwork, “AURA”, and a green play icon

5.8–6.6 seconds:
The selected artwork expands into a large centered cover
Reveal “Glass Tides” underneath, followed by “AURA” in green
Keep the player bar visible
6.6–7.5 seconds:
The same cover slides left
Track information appears on the right:
“Glass Tides”
“AURA”
“A new frequency”
Add a rounded green Play button
Coordinate the cover movement and text reveals
7.5–8.3 seconds:
A brief brand-color transformation fills the inner stage with green
The artwork contracts into a smaller centered tile
Place a small dark Spotify identity underneath
The player briefly recedes
8.3–9.8 seconds:
Return to the dark stage
The same artwork expands dramatically toward the camera, becoming oversized and cropped by the rounded stage
Restore the player at the bottom
Use controlled motion blur during the fastest part of the zoom

9.8–11.2 seconds:
The artwork clears into a centered typographic statement:
“Find your”
“rhythm”
Use white for the first line and green for the second
The player remains visible and stable beneath it
11.2–12.5 seconds:
Show “Made for your every day”
Three playlist sleeves enter with gentle perspective and small opposing tilts
They spread into six smaller sleeves across the stage
Supporting line: “Your sound, always evolving”

12.5–14.0 seconds:
The playlist layout transitions into four floating album covers
Include the iridescent hero artwork
Use restrained rotation, perspective, depth ordering, and overlap
Keep their movement coordinated rather than randomly floating
14.0–15.2 seconds:
The covers converge toward the center and fold around a green Spotify icon
The artwork withdraws as the icon becomes the focal point
Fade the player away
The Spotify icon must emerge from the same central position as the converging covers
15.2–18.0 seconds:
The icon moves slightly left and settles beside a large white “Spotify” wordmark
Keep the icon and letters separated throughout the movement
Reveal:
“Discover new music”
“every day”
The first line is white; the second is green
Hold the finished composition cleanly through the end
</timeline>
<persistent_player>
For most of the middle sequence, keep one narrow rounded player bar near the bottom of the inner stage
Include:
Small hero-art thumbnail
“Glass Tides” and “AURA”
Play and skip controls
A thin progress track
A small volume icon
Subdued dark translucent styling with a fine border
This recurring player connects the changing shots
It must remain visually secondary to the artwork
</persistent_player>

<motion_quality>
Match the energy of a tightly edited premium product film
Most visual ideas last approximately one second, but transitions remain smooth
Use continuous acceleration and deceleration
Favor critically damped springs or carefully tuned smooth easing
No repeated bouncing or large elastic overshoots
Preserve the hero artwork’s identity and position relationships through search, album detail, brand tile, and zoom
Use match-position transitions, coordinated scaling, masked reveals, and perspective
Outgoing titles must disappear before incoming titles occupy the same space
Avoid overlapping text, sudden camera resets, long blank intervals, and arbitrary full-frame crossfades
Clip every oversized cover and camera move cleanly to the rounded stage
No particles, shockwave rings, lens flares, camera shake, or unrelated stock footage
</motion_quality>

<audio> Create or select commercially usable electronic music around 120 BPM Use a clean pulse, warm bass, restrained melodic elements, and subtle transition accents Align important entrances, selections, zooms, and the logo reveal with musical events Keep effects quieter than the music No voiceover Do not use copyrighted commercial tracks without permission </audio>
<implementation_and_validation>
Build a deterministic animation driven by absolute time through an async window. seek(t) function
Every transform, opacity, mask, and UI state must be reproducible when seeking frames in any order
Do not depend on live timers, accumulated physics, or CSS transition state during export

Render true 60 fps with spatial antialiasing
Use 3–5 temporal subframe samples per output frame for restrained motion blur
Keep stationary text and artwork sharp
Inspect contact sheets and moving playback
Check the fast heading changes, artwork handoffs, zoom, cover convergence, and final wordmark spacing
Verify evenly spaced frame timestamps and the full 18-second duration
Fix visual defects before delivering the final MP4 and editable source
</implementation_and_validation>

videos.title: PHYLLA language model launch
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Use the attached PHYLLA video as the primary reference. Inspect its compositions, typography, scene changes, motion, and audio before building.
Ask me for any available original image assets, PHYLLA logo, brand fonts, Higgsfield/Katana branding, and soundtrack. Ask only for information that cannot be recovered from the reference.

If I skip anything, use these defaults:

Brand: PHYLLA.
Product descriptor: “NEW LANGUAGE MODEL”.
Ending tagline: “Generative intelligence”.
Duration: 30 seconds.
Frame rate: 24 fps.
Main film: 1920 × 1080.
Showcase version: 2560 × 1536.
Typography: a bold grotesk sans serif paired with a high-contrast italic serif.
Imagery: botanical macro photography, translucent biological forms, pastel sculptural objects, intimate human portraits, and procedural scientific graphics.
Use original assets where available. Otherwise, create suitable still-image replacements that match the reference’s composition, materials, and palette. Keep photographic assets separate from procedural graphics in the project.
</inputs>

<direction>
Create a complete launch film for PHYLLA using Higgsfield Katana and Claude Motion.
The story: a word behaves like a seed. A person supplies it, intelligence responds, and an entire world grows from that small beginning.

The visual language combines luxury beauty editorial, microscopic nature photography, and precise computational graphics. It should feel tactile, intimate, and carefully art-directed.
Alternate between near-black and warm ivory backgrounds. Use soft pink, peach, pale mint, and muted green throughout. Reserve saturated blue, violet, and orange for brief contrast moments.

Starting palette:

Near-black: #080A09.

Charcoal: #141615.

Ivory: #F4EBDD.
Warm white: #EFEFEF.
Pink: #E8A5C7.
Peach: #F0BC9F.
Mint: #BCDCCE.
Muted green: #779B83.
Higgsfield lime: #D1FF17.
Keep lime mostly in branding, selection outlines, and small interface accents.
Use extreme changes in scale: a tiny seed surrounded by black, a frame-filling cell, a close-up of an eye, then an endless field of flowers. Connect these images through repeated circles, spirals, branching structures, and clusters.
Materials matter. Show moist soil, fine plant fibers, translucent membranes, matte seed shells, natural skin, and softly shaded spheres. Preserve texture. Avoid making everything glossy.

Use bold sans serif for the main sentence and italic serif for the emotional or organic word:
“Everything alive starts small.”
“A seed.”
“A cell.”
“A word.”
“You bring the seed.”
“It grows toward you.”
“Word by word.”
“Plant a word.”
“Watch a world grow.”

Emphasize small, seed, cell, word, you, and world with the italic face where shown in the reference. Use pink italic against black and dark lettering against ivory.

Keep mixed-font baselines and spacing clean. Type should feel designed as part of the composition.

Pacing: begin quietly, build into a quick growth montage, open into larger worlds, then finish with a calm human moment and a clear brand reveal.
Use hard cuts, match cuts, panel expansion, short masked reveals, and controlled camera movement. Do not force the film into a continuous morph.
Avoid generic glitch effects, constant zooming, excessive bloom, elastic text, random interface decoration, and identical movement on every image.
</direction>
<structure>
Build seven chapters on one 720-frame timeline. The timings below are reconstruction targets; refine individual cuts against the reference while keeping the chapter boundaries.
ONE WORD / 0:00–0:04 / frames 0–95
Begin on near-black.
Place a small macro photograph of a pale peach seed in dark soil below and left of center. Give it a thin bounding box, tiny corner handles, a faint elliptical guide, and a small coordinate-style label.
Place “One word.” to its right in bold warm-white text. Leave substantial negative space.
Move toward the seed until its shell, opening, and surrounding soil become prominent. Briefly pair the natural image with a pink point-based reconstruction of the same subject.
During the second half of the chapter, cut through delicate roots, a curled fern, and a pale flowering branch against black.

Show:
“Everything alive
starts small.”

Make small pink and italic. Keep the sentence readable while the imagery changes. Use the recurring branching shapes to connect the cuts.

SMALL BEGINNINGS / 0:04–0:08 / frames 96–191

0:04–approximately 0:04.8:
Cut to ivory. Show a smooth pink-and-peach seed object resting on a softly lit surface. Its two shell-like halves separate slightly to reveal the interior.

Use a soft contact shadow and restrained camera movement. Place “A seed.” large toward the upper-left.
Approximately 0:04.8–0:05.8:
Show a translucent green cell containing soft green clusters and small orange inclusions. Begin with one large cell, then divide the composition into four cells in a precise 2 × 2 arrangement.

Change the text to “A cell.” Add a faint crosshair and a small pink dot diagram.
Approximately 0:05.8–0:06.8:
Cut to black. Reveal a large curved hemisphere made from hundreds of closely packed pastel spheres.

Use pink near the top, peach and cream below, and occasional mint accents. Show enough light and shadow to reveal the individual beads and the curvature of the whole form.

Place “A word.” toward the upper-left. Use a slight orbit or push to reveal depth.

Approximately 0:06.8–0:08:
Create three quick cuts:

Pink and violet ink-like forms with “poems.”

A purple fig cross-section with “recipes.”

A translucent jellyfish in dark water with “answers.”

Use large italic serif text, centered over each image. Keep the words readable despite the quick rhythm.
YOUR SEED / 0:08–0:12 / frames 192–287
Begin on black with a flowering branch. Build an editorial specimen board around it.

Add panels showing:

The natural flowering branch.

A pink dotted reconstruction.
An orange radial cell diagram.

Repeating pink rounded forms.

A pale sculptural flower cluster.
Blue water bordered by pink vegetation.

Use consistent gutters and thin borders. Introduce the panels progressively, with controlled movement and a clear hierarchy.

Around 0:09.75, cut to an open hand against a warm neutral background. Place the small pink seed object in the palm. Preserve natural skin texture, jewelry, and soft lighting.
Let the seed open enough to reveal its warm center.

Show “You bring the seed.” near the upper-left, with seed in italic. Add a small lime input-style label below.

Move to a woman’s side profile on a pale background with soft colored light. Then cut to a dark-background profile, with a fine pink-and-mint branching form extending from her mouth into the empty space.

The branching form represents a spoken idea. Keep it delicate and organic. Preserve the face and expression.
GROWTH / 0:12–0:20 / frames 288–479
Increase the pace.
Approximately 0:12–0:13.75:
A pale green tendril curls around a fingertip against black.

An extreme eye close-up shows natural skin and tiny petal-like flecks.

An orange pollen-bearing structure releases fine particles.

Keep “It grows toward you.” near the lower-left, with you in pink italic.

Approximately 0:13.75–0:15.75:
Pink-and-mint mushrooms on dark moss.
A four-lobed particle form on ivory.
A fuzzy curled fern against black.
Rows of pastel spheres extending into depth.
Give these images different movements. A slow reveal, a restrained rotation, a lateral move, and a deeper push should feel distinct.
Approximately 0:15.75–0:17.75:
Return to a black specimen-board layout.

Show a mint-and-pink dotted root structure beside “Leaf by leaf.”

Expand the layout with a flowering branch, cells, and an orange radial diagram. Change the line to “Word by word.” Make the second word pink and italic.

Build from a simple pair of panels into a richer grid.

Approximately 0:17.75–0:20:
Accelerate through thermal-color botanical or cellular imagery, a pollen burst, and an extreme iris close-up.

Move into the dark pupil. Let the frame become almost black, with a tiny colored point remaining.

Use this brief pause to prepare the next change in scale.

Match shapes across cuts where useful: cell to bead, bead to iris, iris to flower center. Preserve the distinctive material of each subject.

NEW WORLDS / 0:20–0:24 / frames 480–575

Reveal an expansive field of pink and peach flowers on pale ground.
Use ordered repetition, a low camera, soft depth of field, and forward movement. The field should feel much larger than the microscopic world that came before it.
As the scene opens, assemble large black letters into “PHYLLA.” Begin with slightly offset letters, then resolve them into a strong, stable wordmark across the lower-middle of the frame.
Place a small dark label beneath:
“NEW LANGUAGE MODEL”

Keep the text sharp while the flower field moves behind it.

Follow with quick cuts through:
A blue river between dense pink trees.
A path beneath a flowering canopy.
An ivory branching sculpture covered in pink and peach blossoms.
A golden flower center with a clear spiral pattern.

Connect these worlds through palette, branching forms, and radial geometry.

PLANT A WORD / 0:24–0:28 / frames 576–671
Return to black with a large pink dandelion-like seed head.

Show fine fibers, layered structure, and a little mint detail at the center.

Place “Plant a word.” beside it, with word in pink italic.

Push toward the interior. Let the stems create depth without turning the image into an unreadable blur.

Around 0:25.4, cut to a woman’s side profile on ivory. Her eyes are closed. Use soft pink, green, and gold light across her skin, with a small number of floating colored particles.
Place her on the right. Set the final sentence on the left:
“Watch a
world grow.”

Use italic serif for world and bold sans serif for grow. Reveal the phrase cleanly, then hold it.

This should feel quieter and more personal than the growth montage.

PHYLLA / 0:28–0:30 / frames 672–719

Cut to black.

Center a small radial emblem made from pastel spheres, arranged like a flower head or phyllotactic pattern.

Use pink, peach, yellow, and mint. Add subtle rotation or a slight dimensional change.

Place bold white “PHYLLA” beneath it.

Add a smaller pink italic tagline:
“Generative intelligence”
Surround the emblem with very faint concentric arcs. Let the motion settle and hold the complete lockup through the ending.
</structure>

<build>
1. Build the film as an editable, code-driven composition using the supported Katana and Claude Motion workflow. Keep every scene, image, text group, mask, graphic, and audio layer separately adjustable.

Use one deterministic timeline. Derive animation from the current frame or time. Seed procedural randomness so particles, point fields, and layouts remain identical between preview and final render.
Organize the seven chapters as independent scene modules with explicit start and end frames. Allow direct seeking and individual scene renders.
Use still-image plates for photographic material. Create movement with controlled reframing, depth separation, masks, and restrained displacement. Preserve faces, fingers, plant structures, and object proportions.
Build procedural elements where appropriate: sphere arrays, radial bead formations, dot reconstructions, branching lines, grids, crosshairs, arcs, and measurement guides.
For this reconstruction, create the motion and montage within the editable composition. Do not use a video-generation model to produce the finished sequence. Record photographic asset sources separately from procedural elements.

Build typography as editable text. Keep the sans serif and italic serif segments in aligned groups, with consistent baseline behavior and optical spacing.

Use motion blur selectively on fast camera movement and graphic transitions. Preserve readable text and sharp held frames. Do not blur every layer equally.

Add scientific overlays sparingly:

Hairline crosshairs.

Dotted guides.

Sparse ruler ticks.

Small corner handles.

Partial concentric circles.
Compact monospace labels.
Anchor overlays to the subject or composition. Their purpose is to suggest observation and construction.

Create a clean 1920 × 1080 export and a separate 2560 × 1536 showcase export from the same timeline.

For the showcase, use this approximate layout:

videos.title: Escape the orbit kinetic type
videos.prompt:
Create a 20.00-second kinetic typography film titled “ESCAPE THE ORBIT,” based on John F. Kennedy’s Rice University address, September 12, 1962.

The central experience: a sentence discovers that it can change its own trajectory.

Deliver one complete, self-contained HTML file. Composition: 1080×1080. Target: 60fps. Use Canvas, SVG, or embedded WebGL. Embed required assets and libraries. The film must work without audio.

EXACT DISPLAY TEXT
“We choose to go to the moon”
“[…]”
“not because they are easy,”
“but because they are hard”
Preserve this order. The bracketed ellipsis explicitly indicates omitted speech. Attribution is separate from the excerpt. No additional slogans.
ART DIRECTION
Background: midnight # 080D23.
Primary type: warm white # FFF4DD.
Trajectory: electric coral # FF654F.
Secondary orbital geometry: blue # 6685FF.
Use a broad, confident grotesque for the speech and a sharply drawn italic for the final emphatic word. Avoid the appearance of a spacecraft dashboard. No rockets, astronaut illustrations, starfield wallpaper, lens flares, or decorative telemetry.
The frame should resemble an exceptionally refined astronomical instrument that has become expressive.

CENTRAL VISUAL RULE
The baseline of the sentence is a trajectory.

At first it is trapped in a closed orbit. A rhetorical decision changes that orbit into an open path. The letters remain the same travelers throughout.
Use an abstract orbital metaphor; do not present invented mission data or imply a physically accurate flight simulation.
STORYBOARD
0.00–3.50
The opening excerpt appears across the center, large and horizontal. Reveal it in three meaningful phrase groups.
A single hairline ellipse passes behind the baseline. A small circular lunar mark occupies its distant focus.
Hold the completed phrase motionless for 700ms.

3.50–6.00
The camera pulls back. The previously straight baseline reveals a shallow curvature.

The phrase travels along the ellipse as a coherent unit. Keep its glyphs upright during the initial movement. Only after the reading hold may they progressively adopt the tangent of the path.

The viewer realizes the sentence is circling rather than advancing.
6.00–7.00
Show the bracketed omission in an uncluttered central opening. The orbital movement decelerates.

7.00–10.50
Reveal the next clause on the near side of the orbit. Its final word travels through one smooth, effortless arc and returns toward where it started.

This ease should feel elegant but unproductive. Avoid comic bouncing.

10.50–14.50
Reveal the final clause horizontally before transforming it.
At its emphasis, the ellipse opens at one precise point. The same tracked letter group takes the new tangent and departs.
Perform one deliberate 70-degree camera roll. Counter-rotate the active phrase so it remains readable while the orbital field changes orientation around it.

The trajectory sweeps from lower left to upper right. Acceleration is conveyed by expanding spacing between its trailing marks, not by shaking the camera.

14.50–17.00
The camera matches the departing phrase’s velocity. The phrase becomes visually still while the old orbit recedes beneath it.

The lunar mark enlarges into a restrained crescent through geometric overlap. The crescent brackets the destination without becoming a cartoon illustration.
17.00–20.00
Resolve into a spacious editorial composition containing the selected excerpt in reading order, including its omission marker.

The open trajectory runs through the margins and exits the frame. Hold the entire image completely still for the final 1.2 seconds.

CHOREOGRAPHY
Use only three camera operations: pullback, roll, velocity match.
Give each operation a rhetorical purpose.
Keep the currently read phrase at least 64px high in the 1080px composition.
Motion blur may affect trailing geometry, never the active text.
No word may begin its ornamental travel before its reading hold finishes.

IMPLEMENTATION
Represent the ellipse and departure path analytically. Blend position and tangent continuously at the departure point; no teleportation.
Use arc-length sampling for consistent spacing along curves.
Separate camera transforms from glyph orientation.
Cache glyph rendering and static geometry.
Expose window.ready and window. seek(t). Seeking must pause playback and render any time from 0 through 20 deterministically, including out-of-order calls.
Provide window.frame(n) for n=0…1199 at t=n/60.
Render t=20 as the final held composition.
Use no accumulated physics or runtime randomness.

QUALITY GATE
Inspect frames at 0, 3, 5, 7.5, 10.5, 13, 16, and 19 seconds.
Verify that the same tracked phrase visibly follows its own trajectory.

videos.title: Product promo motion template
videos.prompt:
<role>
you design and build motion videos entirely in code, with gsap for the animation and three.js for any 3d. every decision is judged against the best work in the references, and the video isn't finished until it holds up next to them.
</role>

<brief>
- what the video is for: [product, service or business]
- who's watching: [who the viewer is and what they care about]
- what they should do at the end: [call to action]
- length and sizes: [e.g. 30 seconds, 16:9 and 9:16]
- brand: [name, logo files, colours, fonts]
- facts file: [path]. this is the only source for any number, name or claim that appears on screen
- assets: [footage, photos, screenshots, product files]
- style references: [links or a folder of videos whose motion i like]

i'm away and won't answer questions. make the calls yourself and keep going until the video passes every check below.
</brief>

<kit>
before anything else, clone and read https://t.co/FMs1prnPP0. read SKILL.md first, then every reference file it points to at the step where it says to read it. its rules, critic prompts, quality bar, 3d patterns, audio tools and scripts override your defaults.
</kit>

<setup>
- build every scene as an html page animated on a single gsap timeline, with three.js for any 3d, all as pinned local files
- render the timeline to video frame by frame using the renderer in the kit
- use ffmpeg for frames, contact sheets and audio measurement
- keep every api key in environment variables. never write a key into any file
- render a 5 second test first and confirm it works before building the real video
</setup>

<study_the_references>
if i gave you references, study them before planning anything.
- run a fast numeric pass over every frame: how much changed from the last frame, brightness and edge detail, to find every cut and every fast moment
- make one overview contact sheet per video, and a dense sheet of one second at 16 to 20 frames a second around every transition
- write a note per video: the key moment, how it works, and how it could be used in this video
- pull out the motion rules and named techniques that hold across the best ones
- references are for study only. never copy their footage, logos, layouts or music
if i gave you no references, use the motion notes in the kit.
</study_the_references>

<motion_principles>
1. the thing in the front of the shot becomes the transition. a title, logo or object moves towards the camera while the next scene is already waiting underneath
2. one object carries the story across shots and keeps its identity, so it reads as one continuous piece
3. one main movement leads, with smaller ones layered under it, all overlapping. the frame never stops and starts all at once
4. the speed always changes. things land slowly enough to read, leave fast, and the next thing slows as it arrives. no linear motion
5. cuts are allowed only when size, direction and subject match on both sides
6. every action produces a visible result. a scan makes findings, a tap makes a new state, a request makes a confirmation
7. type is motion too. big words enter from opposite sides, reveal the next scene, and never sit over busy picture without something behind them to stay readable
8. vary the scale from close, to wide, to overhead, to full-frame type. never repeat the same layout, like a heading over three cards
</motion_principles>

<storyboard>
write a brief and a storyboard before any animation.
- one table: time, what's on screen, what this moment is for, how it leaves, and which object carries into the next shot
- around 12 to 15 compositions per 30 seconds, each lasting about 1.4 to 3.5 seconds
- the main subject fills most of the frame. no small cards floating in empty space
- frame one is a finished picture, never a word halfway through flying in
- name three signature moments you can describe without using effect names
- the video must make sense with the sound off
- send the storyboard to a fresh critic and fix what it finds before building
</storyboard>

<build>
- every animated value is a function of timeline time only. no timers, no real-time animation, no unseeded randomness. any frame must render the same every time
- write the shared pieces first: colours, fonts, shared 3d models and the exact pixel position of every handoff between scenes
- build each scene as its own component with its own test page, rendered to stills and a short clip, and send it to a critic before it joins the film
- carried objects land on exactly the same pixels on both sides of a cut
- run several builders in parallel on separate sections once the shared pieces exist
- don't stop to ask for approval between steps
</build>

<3d>
- only use 3d where it explains something physical or spatial, like layers, parts, placement or scale
- light it like a product shoot, with a soft key light from one side and a rim light behind
- keep the camera between about 35 and 55 degrees. never look straight down on a large surface, and never end tight on a flat one
- style buildings like a premium architectural model with real materials and a base
- no floating parts, no gaps where parts meet, no flat black glass, no repeating textures
- labels are html positioned from the 3d scene every frame, never text inside the 3d
- measure the rendered background pixel and adjust until it matches the brand colour
- anything that moves like a real product is measured from real footage frame by frame, and those measurements are the curve
</3d>

<images_and_footage>
- prefer building shots in code. use generated images or clips only for supporting shots, and label anything generated as a concept
- upscale and smooth any generated clip to match the rest, and regenerate anything that warps
- never generate a fake finished job, fake customer, fake review or fake result
</images_and_footage>

<audio>
- match the music's energy to the picture and the viewer, and keep it low
- prefer clean library music and sound effects over generated ones. never name a brand in a music prompt
- one short, soft whoosh per real scene change, and small clicks or pops only on real on-screen actions
- screen effects for boom, hiss and length before using them, and set each one just above the music in its own frequency range, with a cap so nothing gets harsh
- cut every scene change on a beat
- always export a music-only version
</audio>

<critic_loop>
the builder never judges its own work.
- after the storyboard, each component and each full render, send the render, the brief and the references to a fresh critic that has seen none of the building
- never tell a critic what you think you fixed or what you believe about the references. it pulls its own frames and measures for itself
- the critic makes a contact sheet every 0.2 seconds plus dense frames around every transition, measures frozen time and loudness, and returns a ranked list of problems with timestamps, ending with ship or one more pass
- fix the biggest problem first, render, then send to a new critic that checks every previous item as fixed, partly fixed or still there, and hunts for anything new that broke
- keep a ledger of every round: what was found, what changed, and the numbers before and after
</critic_loop>

<quality_bar>
the video isn't done until all of these pass, measured:
- no more than about 1 second of frozen screen per 30 seconds, and no still stretch longer than about half a second
- frame one is a finished composition
- all text meets at least 4.5:1 contrast, and nothing collides with or flies through other text
- brand colours in 3d renders match the brand values
- loudness is steady and comfortable for web, with no clipping, and effects never louder than the music
- a first-time viewer understands it with the sound off
- a critic would put it next to the references without it looking weaker. a video with no bugs is not the same as a good video

videos.title: White dot UI motion system
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a target value for the slider, three short notification messages, a reply to type, one accent color and a royalty-free track around 120 BPM. If I skip anything, use 100, "Slider - Reached 100", "Gravity - Something is falling", "Messages - What now?", "retry" and electric blue.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 10-second 2D UI motion film in 16:9. Place everything on a near-black canvas with a faint dot grid. Use charcoal controls, sharp white text, one blue accent and a white ball that moves through the entire film. A real cursor makes the opening click feel physical; the ball guides each transition that follows. Keep the UI clean and the impacts precise, with only small spring overshoots. Move the camera through one continuous layout so every interaction fills the frame.

Banned: hard cuts, stock footage, glows, particle bursts, disconnected transitions, excessive bouncing and blurry text during camera moves.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 10 seconds, with something happening on every major beat.

Toggle: the cursor clicks a blue switch. Its white ball springs free, and the camera follows it toward a horizontal slider.

Slider: the ball lands on the knob and moves it along the track. The blue fill stays attached, while a value bubble above the knob climbs to 100.

Notifications: hitting 100 sends the ball onward and brings in three dark cards: "Slider", "Gravity" and "Messages". Each arrives on its own beat. The camera follows the ball down to "What now?".

Reply: the small "Reply" pill stretches into a text field. A keyboard rises below it as part of the same scene.

Keyboard: the ball strikes the keys while "retry" appears in the field. It lands on Return, the blue send button activates and the reply contracts into a small blue message.

Return: the camera pulls back to show the toggle, slider, cards and keyboard together in one world. The ball travels back to the first switch. Match its position, the cursor and the switch state to the opening frame so the film loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. Make one HTML file at 1920x1080 and 60fps. Calculate every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Arrange all UI components in one world. Use a single camera transform with position and log-space zoom, making each close-up a move through that world.
3. Give the white ball one continuous route between the toggle, slider, cards and keys. Use closed-form springs for landings and a brief squash on impact.
4. Calculate the slider fill and number from the ball's horizontal position. Keep the tooltip centered over the knob until it reaches 100.
5. Give every key press a fixed time. Show the reply as the portion typed by that moment, so any frame can be rendered independently.
6. Align the click, slider movement, card arrivals, key taps, send and return with measured beats. Add a subtle UI sound to each contact.
7. Render one still per beat to check pacing and readability, then export the full film with Playwright at 60fps. Inspect fast camera moves and the loop boundary frame by frame.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never let the ball teleport between components: show the path of every handoff. Keep the value bubble attached to the slider knob. Leave enough space for the notifications to stay readable during camera moves. The keys the ball presses must match the text appearing in the field. Match the first and last frames, including the ball's direction and cursor position, to prevent a loop stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and four stills (toggle, slider, notifications, keyboard) before building the full video.
</start>

videos.title: Orange dot motion system
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a short label for the opening toggle, one hero word, a percentage for the graph, the text for the final card, one accent color, and a track with a clear beat.
</inputs>

<direction>
A 2D motion design film in 16:9. Use a warm off-white canvas, near-black backgrounds, bold typography and one vivid orange accent. The orange dot connects every scene: it starts in the UI, becomes the dot over a letter, traces a spring graph, grows into a shape and returns on the end card. A cursor makes the opening click feel real. Keep the motion sharp and controlled, with small spring overshoots and no dead time.
Banned: stock footage, gradients, glows, particle bursts, random transitions and motion that isn't connected to an element already on screen.
</direction>

<structure>
Around 15 seconds, with a visual change on every major beat.
Open: a cursor clicks the orange toggle beside "Reduce Motion". The letters bend and move into place until only "Motion" remains, with the orange dot above the "i".
Spring: the dot jumps away from the word and lands on a graph. Its path draws a spring response, overshoots the target and settles beside a "+22%" callout.
Shape: the dot shoots across a line, grows into an orange circle and fills the frame. A black rounded square rotates inside it, then stretches into a pill. The scene contracts to a single orange dot on black.
Type: words like "SPRINGS", "EASING", "KINETIC TYPE", "3D" and "SOUND" orbit the dot. The circle of type opens out into a field of tiny dots.
Reveal: the halftone field expands and flips to black, revealing the final card: "Opus 5.5", "Motion designer." and "0 keyframes".
Return: the orange dot moves back through the halftone, graph and toggle. Match the final frame to the first so the video loops cleanly.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080 at 60fps. Compute every visual from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, timers or state carried between frames.
2. Use closed-form springs for the toggle, bouncing dot and graph. Draw the graph from the same spring function that moves the dot.
3. Animate letters individually for the "Reduce Motion" to "Motion" transformation. Keep the orange dot attached to the "i" until it begins its jump.
4. Make the orange circle, rotating square and pill different states of the same shape. Preserve its position and motion through each transformation.
5. Place the orbiting words along a circular path, then move their letters outward to hand the frame over to the halftone grid.
6. Draw the halftone as a grid of dots whose sizes respond to the orange dot. Let it grow past the frame edges before revealing the end card.
7. Sync the click, dot landing, graph peak, shape changes and final title to measured beats. Render one frame per beat to check the pacing before the full export.
</build>

<gotchas>
The graph and dot must follow the same motion or the spring will feel fake. Keep the orange accent consistent across every scene. Give outgoing and incoming text separate timing so letters don't overlap. When a shape fills the screen, scale it past all four corners. Match the cursor, dot and typography in the first and last frames to avoid a loop stutter.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the beat map and four stills (toggle, graph, kinetic type, end card) before building the full video.
</start>

videos.title: Continuous music app morph loop
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the one question a user asks my product and its one-line answer, two album covers, a royalty-free song around 110 BPM with a quiet intro and a hard drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and my logo for the ending. If I skip any, use the defaults: "is this all code?" / "yes. every frame.", two atmospheric photos, Mixkit "Head Bang".
</inputs>

<direction>
A 22 second square loop, 1440x1440 at 60fps, 2D only, one continuous take. Nothing ever cuts: every scene grows out of the last, and every gesture physically carries the camera into the next world. Every morph glides for 0.8s on cubic-bezier(.45,0,.15,1) and the camera zoom rides the same curve, so shapes change so smoothly you barely notice. Content dissolves in the back half of each glide. One gesture per scene.
Look: a warm light stage (#f3f3f0 to #e3e3de), black UI, the app world dark (#121212) tinted from the current album cover, one green accent (#1ed760). Geist for UI, the real macOS pointer, soft layered shadows that grow with the shape's height.
Banned: hard cuts, bouncy springs, particles, glows, zooming in and straight back out, holds longer than 1s, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
Beats are the song's, and the press lands on its drop.
Generate: the cursor clicks, the pill glides into a spinner, then a check.
Chat: the check splits into three typing dots (goo). The left dot flies up into the question bubble and types it, the right one flies down into the reply. Both contract back into dots while gliding in and pour into the middle one.
Play: the middle dot bends into a play triangle, point by point. The cursor presses it on the drop: a white button pops in under the click and the dark app floods out around it, so the leftover white becomes the play button. The camera pulls back to reveal the full now-playing screen: big cover, title, heart (liked, fills green), progress, controls, volume.
Swipe: the cursor drags the cover sideways, the next track slides in, and the whole app retints from the new cover.
Drag: the camera glides to the volume. The cursor drags it to max and keeps pulling: the bar rubber-bands and drags the camera sideways out of the app, tracking the knob across a dark dotted canvas.
Chart: the line lands and bends up into a green chart while the number counts up. The volume knob becomes its last point.
Dive: the cursor clicks that point and the camera dives into it until the light stage fills the frame.
Ending: an "Ask [my product]" button grows out of the light, thins into a line, and the line fans out into my logo (default: the Claude spark, six copies rotating into twelve rays in Claude orange). It folds back into the line, which thickens into Generate. Last frame = first frame.

videos.title: Morphing UI states loop
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

videos.title: Speech built as architecture
videos.prompt: Create a 20.00-second kinetic spoken-word film titled “BUILD THE FLOOR.”  Treat this as an original miniature speech staged entirely through typography. Every line changes the architecture of the frame. The final declaration must stand on something the earlier words physically constructed.  Deliver one self-contained HTML file, 1080×1080, targeting 60fps, using SVG and/or Canvas. Embed all required assets.  ART DIRECTION Background #102820. Paper # F4E9D5. Structural accent # F2B544. A literary editorial world with the scale and confidence of a public monument. Use a high-contrast serif for the speech, a heavy grotesque for load-bearing words, and a restrained monospace for small timing marks. No distressed protest-poster clichés, megaphones, flags, crowds, microphones, or stock footage.  ORIGINAL SPEECH — EXACT WORDS, EXACT ORDER “We were told to wait.” “So we learned the weight of waiting.” “Then one voice made room.” “Then another.” “Now the floor belongs to us.”  Do not attribute these words to any real person. No extra slogans. The complete speech must be understandable without audio.  CENTRAL VISUAL RULE Words have assigned architectural roles. WAIT is a lintel. WAITING is a suspended load. VOICE is a support. ROOM is an opening. FLOOR is a platform. These roles must emerge from the actual letterforms, not from separate illustrations placed behind text.  STORYBOARD 0.00–3.00 “We were told to wait.” The sentence occupies a narrow horizontal opening beneath a massive WAIT. The opening slowly compresses while the sentence remains readable. The pressure comes from the layout, not camera shake.  3.00–6.50 “So we learned the weight of waiting.” Reveal the sentence in spoken phrase groups. WAITING lowers on two fine vertical rules. Those rules become suspension cables. A baseline bends under the visual load using a controlled vector deformation.  6.50–10.00 “Then one voice made room.” VOICE enters vertically and rotates into a structural support. It lifts one end of the baseline. The counter of the O in ROOM becomes an aperture. The next composition is revealed through that aperture.  10.00–12.50 “Then another.” A second support arrives. The tilted structure levels. This is the first moment of perfect horizontal alignment in the film. Use a brief stillness to make the change feel earned.  12.50–16.00 “Now the floor belongs to us.” Earlier structural words assemble into a platform. The final sentence settles onto it. US receives emphasis through shared alignment and scale, never through a separate flashy effect.  16.00–18.00 Hold the complete declaration. A slight release of tension travels through the supporting rules. No new text. No restless decorative motion.  18.00–20.00 The camera tracks beneath the completed platform. Its underside fills the frame and becomes the opening WAIT lintel. Under full occlusion, return hidden elements to their initial positions. Reveal the exact opening composition.  CHOREOGRAPHY Do not force the speech onto a dance beat. Use a cue sheet based on phrases, pauses, and emphasis. Phrase reveals should follow reading order. Allow at least one 400ms moment of absolute stillness. Use critically damped motion for settling loads. Use controlled elastic deformation for the baseline only. Make the changes in available space carry the emotional progression.  TYPE IMPLEMENTATION Use actual glyph paths for structural words. Preserve counters and legibility during deformation. For transitions between unrelated words, use occlusion or matched structural edges; do not interpolate arbitrary path points. Keep the currently spoken phrase readable before it becomes architecture.  ENGINEERING Implement window. seek(t) as a deterministic scene renderer. No accumulated physics, autonomous CSS transitions, or changing random values. Use time-remapping curves and analytic transforms. Use a 20-second periodic timeline with render(0)=render(20). Provide fixed-step access at n/60 for 1200 export frames. Audio is optional and off by default; no browser speech synthesis or autoplay dependency.  QUALITY GATE Inspect eight representative frames. Check that the speech reads in the correct order. Check that structural transformations never destroy a line before the audience can read it. Check the final platform is visibly assembled from earlier elements. Return the complete HTML implementation.

videos.title: Archival brand film with 3D button
videos.prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: a brand name, its logo (SVG or high-res PNG), one line of what it becomes in 5 years (not today's features), one coined word the film should teach (e.g. "signal"), a public-domain archival clip of the old way of doing it (https://t.co/t5EaRxnryq Prelinger), an archived web page from ~2000 where people asked for things (Wayback Machine), a royalty-free song ~100-120 BPM with a real drop (Mixkit, free for commercial use), and a free ElevenLabs key for the narrator (premade voices only).
</inputs>

<direction>
An a16z x Content Rewards brand film, ~55s. It sells one feeling and one idea, never features. Real archival and real web pages, never stock footage, never product screens, never fake UI. One hero object: a 3D button with the logo embossed into it, the ONLY saturated colour in the film. Everything else white, silver, cream and archival black. Small white captions that light up word by word on the narrator's timestamps. Film texture: fresh grain every frame, halation on bright edges, soft vignette, warm lifted blacks. The brand appears at the end, never before.
Banned: stock footage, dashboards, chat UIs, feature tours, cards without real profile pictures, wobbly "worm" graph lines, random glitches, any hold longer than 1.5s, purple, rainbow gradients, orange on anything but the button.
</direction>

<structure>
Cold open (0-8s): the archival clip plays on a glowing old CRT TV with its real dialogue, captions word by word.
The past (8-17s): push into the real 2000 web page, a cursor lands on one real "wanted" post, old pages strobe one per frame, a counter ticks EVERY frame up to today's scale. Narrator: "People have always asked the internet for what they need." / "Today, there are five hundred million posts a day."
Bridge (17-30s): a galaxy of real old asks. One ask snaps to a white outline with a chip of the coined word ("We call that a signal."). Archival of people doing it by hand on the TV. Cut on each word: "Door by door. Call by call. Scroll by scroll." The narrator never stops talking between acts.
Button (30s): the button rises out of black, rim light first, colourless. "[Brand] finds the signals." A flat grey line: "this is how you find customers by hand". Hard cut to a button macro, the colour comes alive, the music drop lands on this exact frame. "and this... is with [Brand]": a steep lit curve, counters changing every frame, a glowing sine with a comet head the camera chases, then platform strikes (X, Reddit, LinkedIn, YouTube, Instagram, TikTok) each with its own counter, then the galaxy again with glowing platform logos: "Every signal on the internet." Hyperspace.
End: the tagline word by word, then "[Brand] is live.", ONE cream frame on the kick, then logo + URL in silence.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, 1920x1080. Everything is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no Math.random (seeded hash), no state between frames.
2. Button: three.js MeshPhysicalMaterial (clearcoat 1, roughness ~0.4), ACES filmic, cool + warm rim spots, room env map. Emboss the real logo by displacing a dense disc with a blurred mask of the logo, folded into the rim so corners don't show. Brushed-metal base.
3. Counters: linear on the film's global clock, so they keep running through cutaways. Tabular numerals, fixed unit label.
4. Captions: <=7 words, one idea per shot, hand-placed line breaks, one text layer on screen at a time. Grey to white over 0.2s on the word timestamps (ElevenLabs /with-timestamps).
5. Glitch = 1-2 frames, only on a real cut, always with a click. Readable things stay on screen >= 8 clean frames.
6. Render with Playwright per frame (Chromium with --use-angle=swiftshader so WebGL renders headless), finish in numpy: fresh grain per frame, halation, vignette ~0.65x at the corners, 1px chroma fringe with EDGE-CLAMPED shifts. Pipe PNGs into ffmpeg, h264, 24fps.
7. Mix: narrator 10-15dB over the music, duck -18dB while speaking, hits on the exact action frame, -14 LUFS.
</build>

<gotchas>
If the narrator pauses, the visuals must not stop. If a counter freezes, the render is broken. If the button isn't the most memorable thing in the film, start over.
</gotchas>
